bodyHtml:
Corrosion under insulation (CUI) in one paragraph

Short answer: Corrosion under insulation (CUI) is external corrosion of piping, vessels and tanks underneath thermal insulation or fireproofing. It happens when water gets past the jacketing and is held against the steel. On carbon and low-alloy steel it shows up as general or localised wall loss. On austenitic and duplex stainless steels the main risk is external chloride stress corrosion cracking (ECSCC). Risk is highest in an intermediate operating temperature band, in intermittent or cyclic service, at penetrations and low points, and in warm, wet or coastal climates.

This section adds the detail owners and inspectors most often ask about: the temperature ranges the codes use, the specific places CUI starts, how the main in-service codes treat it, and how the screening methods compare. Code references are paraphrased. Confirm limits against the current edition of each document before using them in an inspection plan.

CUI temperature ranges: what the codes and references say

Temperature matters because it controls whether water stays at the steel surface. Below roughly freezing, water is ice and corrosion is slow. Well above the boiling point the surface usually stays dry, unless the line cycles or runs intermittently. Between those limits, water that gets in keeps condensing, evaporating and concentrating salts at the surface. That wet-dry cycling is what makes CUI aggressive.

MaterialDamage formBand commonly citedSource and status
Carbon and low-alloy steelGeneral and localised wall loss, pittingAbout 10°F to 350°F (-12°C to 177°C)Attributed to API 510 for insulated vessels (as quoted by Inspectioneering) and widely cited from API RP 571 and RP 583. Confirm in the current edition.
Carbon steel above the bandWall loss during wet periodsAbove the upper limit, in intermittent or cyclic serviceCodes flag intermittent and cyclic service as susceptible regardless of design temperature.
Austenitic and duplex stainless steelExternal chloride SCC (ECSCC)About 140°F to 400°F (60°C to 204°C)Widely cited secondary summary of current references. Confirm in current API RP 583 or RP 571.
Historical referenceCarbon steel wall loss; stainless ECSCCNarrower bands in older code editionsThe 1998 edition of API 570 used narrower bands. Later documents widened them. Do not plan from an old edition.

Three practical points follow. First, the design temperature on the line list is often not the temperature the steel actually sees. Bypassed exchangers, idle spares, start-up lines, dead legs and steam-out connections can sit in the susceptible band for long periods while the design value says "hot". Second, equipment that is normally cold can still be at risk. Cold service below the band can see heavy condensation where insulation or vapour barriers have failed, and lines that warm up during shutdowns pass through the band. Third, the worst attack is generally reported in the middle of the carbon steel band, where water evaporates and re-wets most often. Treat that part of the range as highest priority in a screening plan.

Where CUI starts: a location checklist

CUI is not random. It starts where water can get past the jacket and where it collects. API 570, API 510 and API RP 583 all describe susceptible locations in similar terms. The list below is our own summary for field use:

  • Penetrations through the insulation: nozzles, small-bore branches, vents, drains, instrument connections, steam tracer entries, pipe supports and hangers, ladder and platform clips, and bolted shoes.
  • Insulation terminations: at flanges, valves and fittings, at the ends of insulated runs, and at vertical terminations where water runs down the jacket and into the end.
  • Damaged or degraded jacketing: dents, open seams, missing bands, hardened or cracked caulking, and seams on the top of horizontal runs facing the weather.
  • Low points: the bottom of vertical runs, the six o'clock position on horizontal lines, and vessel skirts and bottom heads where water drains to.
  • Visible symptoms: bulges in the jacket, rust staining, blistered paint at insulation ends, and wet insulation found during maintenance.
  • Water sources nearby: deluge and fire-water systems, cooling tower drift, steam leaks, process leaks, safety showers and wash-down areas.
  • Service conditions: lines in the susceptible band, cyclic or intermittent service, dead legs and lines kept on standby.
  • Coating history: equipment insulated with no coating, or with a coating past its expected life. Insulation itself is not a corrosion barrier.

For tanks and spheres, also look at the shell-to-roof junction under insulation, nozzles and manways, and the bottom course where water drains down the shell.

Climate: why CUI programmes in North America are not all the same

CUI rates follow the climate. Gulf Coast refineries and chemical plants in Texas and Louisiana see warm temperatures, high humidity, heavy rain and marine chlorides, close to the worst combination for CUI. Atlantic coast and Great Lakes sites add freeze-thaw cycling that opens jacket seams. Dry mid-continent and mountain sites generally see less CUI, but deluge testing, steam leaks and cooling tower drift can create local wet zones anywhere. Older API 570 guidance already noted that marine and warm humid sites need more active CUI programmes than dry inland sites. Current RP 583 likewise asks the owner to assess the local environment. In Canada, Alberta oil sands and upgrader sites combine long cold winters with steam-traced and heat-traced lines that cycle. Coastal BC and Atlantic Canada see marine exposure. Climate does not set the interval on its own, but it is a legitimate reason to put one site's screening extent above another's.

How the in-service codes treat CUI

None of the main in-service codes treats CUI as optional, but none hands you a single universal percentage either. In broad terms:

  • API 570 (piping, current 5th Edition, 2024) requires the owner's inspection plan to address CUI for susceptible insulated piping. It ties the extent of follow-up examination to the piping class and to what external visual inspection finds. Check the current edition for the specific extents.
  • API 510 (pressure vessels, 11th Edition) calls for CUI to be considered for externally insulated vessels in the susceptible temperature range or in intermittent service, as part of external inspection planning.
  • API RP 583 is the dedicated recommended practice for corrosion under insulation and fireproofing. It covers design, maintenance, inspection and mitigation for vessels, piping, tanks and spheres, including how to prioritise and select inspection methods. See our RP 583 decoded guide.
  • API RP 571 describes CUI as a damage mechanism: affected materials, critical factors and appearance. It is one of the RP 571 sections listed for the API 510, 570 and 653 certification exams.
  • AMPP (formerly NACE) SP0198 covers controlling corrosion under thermal insulation and fireproofing through coatings, insulation selection and design.

OSHA's PSM rule and EPA's RMP rule do not name CUI. They require mechanical integrity inspection consistent with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and for insulated covered equipment that in practice means a documented CUI approach. Inspection extents and intervals are decisions for the owner and its API inspector under the code. They are not set by the NDE contractor.

CUI inspection methods compared

Most CUI programmes combine a screening step, which finds where to look, with a follow-up step, which measures what is there. Note that pulsed eddy current and profile radiography are two different methods, not one.

MethodRoleWhat it tells youMain limits
External visual of jacketingScreeningDamaged jacket, seams, caulking, staining, bulges, wet areasShows where water can get in, not whether the steel has corroded
Infrared thermographyScreeningWet insulation from thermal contrastDepends on temperature difference and weather; finds water, not wall loss
Profile radiography (film or digital)Screening and measurement on small-bore and medium pipingWall profile and loss at the tangent through the insulationRadiation controls; limited diameter and wall; samples sections, not full coverage
Pulsed eddy current (PEC)Screening through insulation and jacketAverage remaining wall over the probe footprintAverages over an area, so small pits are under-called; ferromagnetic steel only; jacket type and thickness affect results
Guided wave testing (GWT)Screening of long runsCross-sectional loss along tens of metres from one collar locationNeeds a small insulation window; reduced range at bends, supports and with some coatings; screening sensitivity, not thickness
UT thickness and corrosion mapping after insulation removalFollow-up measurementActual minimum thickness and loss pattern for corrosion rate and remaining lifeNeeds insulation removal and surface preparation; coverage only where stripped
Visual, MT and PT after removal; PT for stainlessFollow-up and ECSCC detectionSurface condition, pitting and stainless chloride crackingNeeds access to the bare surface

For carbon steel, screening methods find suspect areas and UT measurement after stripping gives the number the inspector uses. For stainless steel, the concern is cracking, and wall-loss methods such as PEC will not find ECSCC. Plan stripping with dye penetrant at the susceptible locations instead. Our pages on guided wave testing and corrosion mapping cover two of these methods, and CUI detection without removing insulation compares the through-insulation options.

What a defensible CUI record looks like

When an auditor or the API inspector reviews a CUI programme, they look for a chain from susceptibility to decision:

  • a susceptibility list of insulated lines and equipment, with material, actual operating temperature, cyclic or intermittent flags, coating status and environment;
  • external visual results for the jacketing, with photos and locations;
  • screening method, coverage and results, each with procedure and examiner certification;
  • follow-up examination locations chosen from the screening results and the code's targeting logic, with measured thicknesses tied to CMLs;
  • repair and reinstatement records for coating, insulation and jacket;
  • the inspector's evaluation of corrosion rate, remaining life and next inspection date.

If screening data cannot be tied to a CML or a line location, it rarely survives the next turnaround planning cycle.

Common CUI programme mistakes

  • Screening only by design temperature. Actual temperature, idle periods and cycling decide susceptibility.
  • Treating PEC averages as minimum thickness. Prove up PEC calls with UT after stripping before using them in remaining-life calculations.
  • Looking for wall loss on stainless steel. The stainless risk is ECSCC, which needs surface examination.
  • Reinsulating without recoating. Putting wet or uncoated steel back under new insulation resets the clock.
  • Ignoring supports and penetrations. Long straight runs are easy to screen. Many failures start at the details.
  • Planning from an old code edition. Temperature bands and extent tables have changed between editions.

More questions about corrosion under insulation

What is corrosion under insulation (CUI)?

External corrosion or cracking of insulated or fireproofed equipment, caused by water that gets past the jacketing and is held against the metal surface.

At what temperature does CUI occur in carbon steel?

The commonly cited range is about 10°F to 350°F (-12°C to 177°C), plus higher-temperature equipment in intermittent or cyclic service. Confirm the band in the current API 510, 570 or RP 583.

Does stainless steel suffer from CUI?

Yes, mainly as external chloride stress corrosion cracking. It is commonly cited at about 140°F to 400°F (60°C to 204°C) for austenitic and duplex grades.

What is CUI inspection?

A programme that identifies susceptible insulated equipment, screens it with visual and through-insulation methods, and measures suspect areas after insulation removal, so the API inspector can evaluate remaining life.

Which code covers corrosion under insulation inspection?

API 570 and API 510 require CUI to be addressed in inspection plans. API RP 583 is the dedicated recommended practice, and API RP 571 describes the damage mechanism.

How often should insulated piping be checked for CUI?

The interval and extent are set by the owner's inspection programme under API 570 or API 510. They depend on piping class or vessel criticality, external visual findings, past corrosion rates and any risk-based assessment the owner has done. There is no single universal frequency. The NDE contractor supplies the data, and the API inspector sets the interval.

Can CUI be found without removing insulation?

Screening can be done through insulation with profile radiography, pulsed eddy current or guided wave testing. Confirming a minimum thickness for remaining-life calculations normally needs UT after the insulation is removed at the suspect locations. Ask us to plan screening plus follow-up UT.
